source.title: Optimal Initialization in Depth: Lyapunov Initialization and Limit Theorems for Deep Leaky ReLU Networks
source.authors: Constantin Kogler; Tassilo Schwarz; Samuel Kittle

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices; no document problem noted.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares initialization methods and reports learning outcomes in deep networks, using empirical learning accuracy and loss rather than directly measuring the initialization properties in V4.
record.gate_note: The paper reports MNIST test accuracy for seven initialization methods across five epochs, averaged over 100 seeds. These results bear on initialization and learning speed, but do not test training classification error on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, residual shortcuts, or the other claim versions. The polynomial and score experiments also report learning losses, but are not extracted as they do not measure the classification learning behavior named in V1 or V4.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4 in narrow, deep plain Leaky ReLU networks: initialization changes learning curves and training success on MNIST, polynomial regression and score estimation. It also proves that activation-matched second-moment scaling does not prevent typical activation decay at finite width. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct but incomplete. The authors establish finite-width activation-growth theory and conclude that zero-exponent Lyapunov initialization improves learning in narrow, deep Leaky ReLU networks. Sampling helps early MNIST learning but does not retain its advantage at epoch 200; at epoch 15 sampled Gaussian still exceeds unsampled Gaussian, 52% versus 49%. Polynomial and score experiments also favor the proposed methods, particularly sampled orthogonal initialization.
record.recipe_differences: The paper proposes Lyapunov and sampled Lyapunov initialization and compares them with standard initializations; the experiments use AdamW on MNIST rather than the claim versions’ benchmark setups.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization method and training epoch affect reported test accuracy; sampled methods outperform corresponding unsampled methods at epochs 1 and 5, but unsampled Lyapunov methods perform better at higher epochs.
record.problems: The MNIST experiment reports test accuracy rather than training classification error. Results are averaged over 100 seeds, but no uncertainty estimates are given. The authors note that they selected hyperparameters by mean final validation accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: The polynomial learning and score learning experiments are not extracted: they report regression or score-estimation losses rather than the classification learning behavior named by the versions. Their results appear in Sections 5, H, and I, and Figures 4, 7, 9, and 10.

untested.parts: CIFAR training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and size or regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious minima frequency and extra student neurons.
Depth comparisons, batch-normalized convolutional networks, identity shortcuts and Fixup.

Gradient propagation is not directly measured; no empirical depth sweep, very deep tanh comparison, equal-variance tanh orthogonal/Gaussian comparison, or 10,000-layer convolutional training. MNIST reports test accuracy rather than training loss or classification error.
Learning rates relative to stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, catapult recovery and edge-of-stability training.
Normalization comparisons, higher-learning-rate tolerance and Fixup.

missing.what: Finite-width qualification to signal preservation: standard He and scaled orthogonal weights preserve activation second moments but have negative typical growth rates. At width 10 and slope 0.1, the exponents are -0.1445718 and -0.0929117; both approach zero as width increases. Zero Lyapunov exponent removes exponential drift but leaves depth-dependent fluctuations.
missing.locator: Sections 3–4, Theorems 3.3–3.4 and 4.1–4.3; Appendix D.3, Table 2; Appendix F

missing.what: MNIST seed distributions distinguish failed optimization from lower accuracy among successful runs. At epoch 200, median accuracies are 11.5% for He, 86.4% for standard orthogonal and 88.3% for Lyapunov orthogonal, despite means of 36.0%, 59.6% and 84.1%. These distributions materially clarify the mean-only rows.

record.verdict_notes: All 35 MNIST values match Figure 3. Their states describe learning within the initialization comparison, not whether each method is best. The later sampling reversal is not a limits_scope verdict on V4, which makes no sampling-superiority claim. Polynomial and score losses also bear on V4: it is not restricted to classification. They are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. Comparisons use separately tuned hyperparameters; polynomial summaries additionally select the best 80% of seeds. Zero-exponent scaling does not guarantee bounded activations or successful learning for every seed.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 training classification error, corrupted or random labels, model size, early stopping, and regularized recipes.
Two-layer teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious minima frequency, and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual networks, depth-related training error, shortcuts, and training without normalization.

The empirical experiment uses Leaky ReLU networks on MNIST, not the very deep tanh or convolutional settings in the version; it does not test orthogonal versus Gaussian weights at equal variance or train 10,000-layer networks.
Learning rates above a stability threshold, curvature or sharpness dynamics, and divergence.
Batch normalization versus no normalization and tolerance to higher learning rates.

relationships.reason: R8–R14 show epoch-5 accuracy of 12% for Glorot, 23% for He and 31–44% for Lyapunov variants; R29–R35 show 12%, 36% and 70–84% respectively at epoch 200.
relationships.display_finding: At epoch 5, accuracy was 12% for Glorot, 23% for He and 31–44% for Lyapunov variants; at epoch 200, these reached 12%, 36% and 70–84%, respectively.

relationships.condition: Standard activation-matched He and scaled orthogonal initialization at finite, low width
relationships.reason: Text-only theory in Sections 3–4 proves typical activation decay despite preserved second moments; R30–R33 show corresponding mean accuracies of 36%/60% versus 76%/84% after corrected scaling. Activation matching alone therefore needs a finite-width qualification.
relationships.display_finding: Theory proved typical activation decay despite preserved second moments, and corrected scaling raised mean accuracies from 36% and 60% to 76% and 84%, respectively.

relation.reason: Its theory directly examines activation propagation under standard initialization, and its experiments compare learning under different initializations.

tranche.reason: The study extends V4 to narrow, deep Leaky ReLU networks, with finite-width activation theory and initialization-dependent learning results in new experimental settings.

source_check.notes: The theory concerns forward activation norms, not gradient preservation; the MNIST comparison fixes depth rather than measuring depth-dependent startup. Accuracies use separately tuned hyperparameters and 100 seeds; zero Lyapunov exponent still permits depth-dependent stochastic fluctuations.
